query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a homogeneous, metastable solid-solution state, thermal activation (as experienced during service) induces a degree of chemical short‐range ordering that locally enriches Mg and triggers the precipitation of Mg‐rich intermetallic compounds—primarily at grain boundaries. These precipitates in turn modify the alloy’s ability to form a continuous, protective oxide scale at high temperatures and alter local electrochemical properties, thereby leading to either enhanced or degraded corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Mg-containing lightweight HEA in a metastable, non-equilibrium solid-solution state with uniform distribution of Mg and other principal elements
generation.intervention: Application of controlled thermal aging (heat treatment) simulating high-temperature service conditions
generation.conditions: Service-relevant regimes including high-temperature oxidation (e.g., temperatures above 500°C) and corrosive environments (e.g., immersion in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution), with controlled aging durations
generation.structural_mediator: Precipitation of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds at grain boundaries facilitated by thermally induced chemical short-range order
generation.mechanism: Heat treatment promotes local chemical ordering that drives Mg segregation; once a critical local concentration is reached, Mg-rich intermetallic phases nucleate and grow. If these precipitates are finely dispersed and coherent, they may help nucleate a protective oxide layer that sustains oxidation resistance. Conversely, if the intermetallics coarsen or become discontinuous, they can act as galvanic sites or discontinuities in the protective film, leading to a reduction in corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-solid-solution state, thermally aged samples will show the emergence of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries. In samples where the precipitates remain small and uniformly dispersed, a continuous protective oxide film may form—retaining oxidation and corrosion resistance. In contrast, samples that develop coarse or uneven intermetallic distributions will show measurable decreases in corrosion resistance due to localized galvanic effects and disruption of oxide film continuity.
generation.baseline: The initial metastable solid solution state exhibits a uniform microstructure with excellent corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance due to the even element distribution and absence of detrimental intermetallic phases.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable under service conditions involving high temperatures (e.g., >500°C) and aggressive environments (e.g., chloride-containing media). The kinetics of SRO formation and intermetallic precipitation depend on heat treatment duration and temperature, with insufficient aging failing to trigger significant changes and excessive coarsening potentially degrading protective properties.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise processing window at which intermetallic precipitation transitions from beneficial (by promoting protective oxide formation) to detrimental (by creating galvanic couples). The extent and morphology of intermetallic formation may vary with minor processing parameter changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples. Subject one set to a controlled thermal aging regimen (e.g., exposure to temperatures >500°C for selected durations) while keeping the second set in the as-solid-solution state. Then, perform microstructural characterization (using SEM/TEM) to assess intermetallic precipitate formation and carry out standardized corrosion (potentiodynamic polarization and impedance spectroscopy in 3.5 wt.% NaCl) and high-temperature oxidation (using thermogravimetric analysis or cyclic oxidation testing) measurements.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM imaging, EDS mapping) to quantify the presence, morphology, and location of Mg-rich intermetallic phases
Electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization and impedance spectroscopy) to assess corrosion resistance
Oxidation weight gain and oxide scale characterization to evaluate oxidation resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermal aging does not induce a statistically significant increase in Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates compared to the as-solid-solution state, and if the measured corrosion and oxidation resistances remain unchanged (or improve uniformly) regardless of the treatment, then the proposed mechanism linking SRO-induced intermetallic precipitation to altered corrosion/oxidation behavior is falsified.

Effects of Alloying Elements and Mechanical Alloying on Characteristics of WVTaTiCr Refractory High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are among the promising candidates for the design of structural materials in advanced nuclear energy systems. The effects of Cr, V, Ta, and Ti elements and ball milling on the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of model RHEAs were investigated. The results show that W-rich BCC1 and Ta-rich BCC2 solid solution phases were generated after a long milling duration. After high-temperature sintering, the (Cr, Ta)-rich phase associated with the Laves phase was observed in the Cr-containing model RHEAs. In addition, a high level of Ti, Ta, and V contents promoted the in situ formation of oxide particles in the alloys. Complex TiTa2O7 and Ta2VO6 oxide phases were identified by TEM, which suggests a solid-state reaction of Ti-O, Ta-O, and V-O subjected to high-energy ball milling. The oxide particles are uniformly dispersed in the BCC matrix, which can result in dispersion strengthening and the enhancement of mechanical properties.

Nonequilibrium chemical short-range order in metallic alloys

Abstract: AbstractMetallic alloys are routinely subjected to nonequilibrium processes during manufacturing, such as rapid solidification and thermomechanical processing. It has been suggested in the high-entropy alloy literature that chemical short-range order (SRO) could offer a new knob to tailor materials properties. While evidence of the effect of SRO on materials properties accumulates, the state of SRO evolution during alloy manufacturing remains obscure. Here, we employ high-fidelity atomistic simulations to track SRO evolution during the solidification and thermomechanical processing of alloys. Our investigation reveals that alloy processing can lead to nonequilibrium steady-states of SRO that are different from any equilibrium state. The mechanism behind nonequilibrium SRO formation is shown to be an inherent ordering bias present in nonequilibrium events. These results demonstrate that conventional manufacturing processes provide pathways for tuning SRO that lead to a broad nonequilibrium spectrum of SRO states beyond the equilibrium design space of alloys.Subject terms: Atomistic models, Metals and alloys This

The Effect of Scandium Ternary Intergrain Precipitates in Al-Containing High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: We investigate the effect of alloying with scandium on microstructure, high-temperature phase stability, electron transport, and mechanical properties of the Al2CoCrFeNi, Al0.5CoCrCuFeNi, and AlCoCrCu0.5FeNi high-entropy alloys. Out of the three model alloys, Al2CoCrFeNi adopts a disordered CsCl structure type. Both of the six-component alloys contain a mixture of body-centered cubic (bcc) and face centered cubic (fcc) phases. The comparison between in situ high-temperature powder diffraction data and ex situ data from heat-treated samples highlights the presence of a reversible bcc to fcc transition. The precipitation of a MgZn2-type intermetallic phase along grain boundaries following scandium addition affects all systems differently, but especially enhances the properties of Al2CoCrFeNi. It causes grain refinement; hardness and electrical conductivity increases (up to 20% and 14% respectively) and affects the CsCl-type → fcc equilibrium by moving the transformation to sensibly higher temperatures. The maximum dimensionless thermoelectric figure of merit (ZT) of 0.014 is reached
